Imagine stepping into a world where the pursuit of justice and equality shapes every moment. That’s the world brought to life by Ruth Bader Ginsburg—someone whose legacy didn’t just challenge the boundaries of gender and law, but actually reshaped them.
What does it take to move from being a quiet, determined student to becoming a Supreme Court Justice? Well, as we’ll discover together, it’s a story of resilience, sharp intellect, and the kind of courage that stands tall, even in the face of deeply rooted discrimination.
Through the pages of Notorious RBG: The Life and Times of Ruth Bader Ginsburg, written by Irin Carmon, we get to walk alongside Ginsburg as she evolves into a true cultural icon. We’ll dig into the origins of her unshakable commitment to fairness, and look at the legal strategies that didn’t just win cases—they transformed the American landscape.
Ginsburg’s journey isn’t just about her own triumphs. It’s really about all of us, and about a much bigger movement toward dignity and equal rights. Along the way, you’ll hear how her landmark cases and unforgettable dissents reached far beyond the courtroom, and how her life blended public and private battles with a sense of real urgency and inspiration.
What makes her story so compelling is the way her personal beliefs fuelled her professional victories. Together, we’ll see how principled leadership, meticulous reasoning, and a fierce sense of justice can create a legacy that inspires generations to challenge what’s possible.
As we explore her early influences and her lasting mark on law and culture, one thing becomes crystal clear—Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s vision is as relevant today as it’s ever been. So, let’s dive in and discover what makes her story so powerful, and why her impact continues to echo in our world.

Early Lessons in Strength and Fairness.
Before anyone ever knew the name Ruth Bader Ginsburg, there was just a quiet girl in Brooklyn, taking in the world from a small apartment filled with the smells of home-cooked meals and the gentle buzz of family conversations.
Picture a young Ruth, watching her mother move through each day with a kind of determined grace. Her mother had set aside her own dreams of education, but she poured all her hopes into Ruth—teaching her that independence and learning weren’t just nice to have, they were absolutely essential.
School quickly became Ruth’s second home. She’d sit up near the front, not to be the center of attention, but just to soak up every single word the teacher said. At night, she’d stay up late, pouring over her books, convinced that knowledge could open doors that most people never even saw. Her mother was her biggest supporter, always there with encouragement—but she was also firm about discipline and self-control. In a world that kept telling girls to stay quiet, Ruth learned to listen deeply, to choose her words carefully, and never to let anger get the best of her.
Then, loss came early. Just as Ruth was about to graduate from high school, her mother became seriously ill. The days at home grew heavy, and the apartment felt emptier with each passing week. The day before graduation, Ruth’s mother passed away. Instead of letting her grief swallow her, Ruth held onto those lessons—resilience, self-control, and fairness—turning them into a quiet strength that would shape her whole life.
When Ruth arrived at college, it felt like stepping into a brand-new world—one full of possibility, but also full of reminders that women were still expected to know their place. At Cornell, she found brilliant classmates, but she also noticed how the women were often expected to look for husbands rather than careers. Professors sometimes seemed to overlook her, calling on a male student even when her hand was up. But Ruth didn’t let that stop her. She found mentors who saw her potential, and she excelled.
And then she met Marty—a fellow student whose quick humor and warmth stood out right away. Their partnership wasn’t just about love; it was built on a real belief in each other’s abilities and dreams.
The world outside was changing, but it was slow. Ruth could see that the law could either keep old barriers in place—or help tear them down. She started to imagine a future where her mind and her efforts could make things a little bit fairer, not just for herself, but for everyone who’d ever been told to wait their turn.
Looking back, you can see how these early years—shaped by hardship, hope, and a mother’s unwavering belief—planted the seeds for everything Ruth Bader Ginsburg would go on to do.

Breaking Barriers in Law School and Family Life.
Law school in the 1950s wasn’t exactly a place that rolled out the welcome mat for women. When Ruth showed up at Harvard, she was one of only a few women in a sea of hundreds of men. The message was loud and clear—she didn’t really belong.
Imagine this: the dean invites the women to dinner, and instead of a warm welcome, he asks why they think they deserve to take a man’s place. That’s the kind of moment that could make anyone want to disappear. But not Ruth. She just sat up, a little taller, determined to prove she absolutely belonged there.
The obstacles kept coming. Study groups often left her out, and sometimes professors dismissed her questions without a second thought. But Ruth? She had her own way of doing things. She pored over every single case, prepared down to the smallest detail, and let her work speak for itself.
Home wasn’t any less challenging. Marty, her husband, was also in law school, and when he got seriously ill, Ruth’s world became a delicate balancing act. She cared for their young daughter, managed the house, and kept up with coursework for both herself and Marty. Nights blurred into mornings as she typed up Marty’s papers after finishing her own—running on coffee, determination, and love for her family.
Most people would’ve cracked under all that pressure, but Ruth found her rhythm. She learned how to focus on one thing at a time, to lean on the rare people who truly supported her, and to keep moving forward. When Marty recovered, it was a huge relief—but it also deepened their sense of partnership. He was her biggest cheerleader, never threatened by her ambition, always ready with a joke to lighten the mood. Their marriage was a real partnership—something you didn’t see much back then—and it gave Ruth the confidence to keep reaching higher.
When Marty’s job took them to New York, Ruth transferred to Columbia and graduated at the very top of her class. But even with all those credentials, doors stayed shut. Law firms wouldn’t hire her, judges turned down her clerkship applications—all because she was a woman and a mother. That’s when Ruth realized: talent alone wasn’t going to be enough. The system itself was set up to keep women out.
Instead of letting bitterness take over, she turned to a new path. Ruth found work as a researcher and teacher, diving deep into the ways law treated men and women differently. Every setback became fuel for her growing sense of purpose.
During these years, Ruth’s understanding of justice really took root. She saw how the law could be both a shield and a weapon, and she started to imagine how it could open doors for people who’d always found them closed.
The lessons of persistence, true partnership, and quiet determination? They became her trademarks—guiding the way she’d go on to fight for change, not just for herself, but for everyone after her.

Chapter 3: Fighting for Equality in the Courts
By the time the 1970s rolled around, the world was really starting to change. The women’s movement was picking up steam, and the law was—finally—beginning to catch up. Ruth, now teaching law, saw a chance to make an impact—not just in the classroom, but in the courtroom too.
She teamed up with advocates who were challenging laws that treated men and women differently. Sometimes, those differences seemed tiny on paper, but they ended up having huge consequences in real life.
Take one case Ruth worked on—a widower who was denied Social Security benefits simply because the law assumed only women needed help when their spouse died. Sound fair? Ruth didn’t think so. She saw the real harm, and not just for women. Men, too, were boxed in by these old stereotypes.
So, Ruth crafted her arguments in a way that made judges stop and listen. She explained how gender discrimination hurts everyone—not just one side. And, she did it with this calm, logical style that stood out in court. No shouting, no grandstanding—just a steady voice and crystal-clear reasoning. She let the facts and the law speak for themselves.
Winning wasn’t easy. The legal system is notorious for being slow to change, and many judges were, let’s be honest, pretty skeptical. But Ruth was patient and strategic. She picked her cases carefully, aiming for ones that could set powerful precedents and slowly build a foundation for broader change.
Every win—no matter how small—chipped away at those old assumptions. And each one made it tougher for the law to keep ignoring the real lives and needs of people.
Outside the courtroom, Ruth was just as dedicated. She mentored students and young lawyers, always encouraging them to think deeply and see the law as something alive—something that could grow and change. She also balanced all this with family life, finding happiness in quiet moments with Marty and their kids. The demands were huge, but she handled them with the same careful discipline that got her through every challenge before.
As more people noticed her work, Ruth’s influence grew—not just because of her sharp legal mind, but because of her empathy. She had a rare ability to connect with folks from all walks of life. She knew that real change took more than just court wins; it needed cultural shifts too. So, she worked hard to build bridges between legal victories and everyday lives.
The fight for equality wasn’t over—not by a long shot. But Ruth had become one of its most effective champions. She proved that with persistence and smart strategy, even the toughest barriers could start to move.

Chapter 4: Becoming a Judge and Shaping the Law
Imagine spending years as a passionate advocate—fighting for what you believe in—and then stepping into a new role where your job isn’t to convince, but to decide. That’s exactly what happened when Ruth was appointed to the federal bench. The shift from advocate to judge wasn’t easy. Suddenly, she had to set her personal views aside and focus on applying the law as fairly as possible, even when it challenged her own beliefs.
Ruth handled this transition with the same careful dedication that had defined her entire career. She read every brief, weighed every argument, and made sure her opinions were not just thorough, but crystal clear. If you’ve ever tried to write something that’s both precise and easy to understand, you know just how much work that can be.
On the bench, Ruth earned a reputation for being deeply collegial. She listened—really listened—to her colleagues, and looked for common ground wherever she could find it. But here’s the thing: she never compromised her core principles. If she disagreed with a decision, she didn’t just grumble about it. She explained her reasoning thoughtfully and respectfully, always hoping to persuade others—or at the very least, to lay the groundwork for future change.
One thing that set Ruth apart was the way she focused on the real-world impact of the law. She never lost sight of how decisions would actually affect people’s lives—especially those who were often overlooked. For Ruth, the law wasn’t just a collection of rules. It was a tool for justice. And that perspective earned her respect, even from folks who didn’t always agree with her.
Ruth’s empathy came, in part, from her own experiences as an outsider. She remembered what it felt like to be excluded—and she brought that understanding to her work. She balanced emotion with reason, always careful not to let one overshadow the other. Her opinions were logical and clear, but they also showed a real awareness of the challenges people faced.
As word of her thoughtful approach spread, so did Ruth’s influence. She became a role model for young lawyers—especially women—who saw in her a path they could follow. She proved that you could be both principled and pragmatic, that you could keep fighting for change while also knowing when to compromise.
In so many ways, Ruth’s work as a judge paved the way for her future on the Supreme Court, where her impact would only grow stronger.

Chapter 5: Joining the Supreme Court and Building a Legacy
Imagine working your whole life toward something, and then—finally—reaching that moment. That’s what it was like for Ruth when she was nominated to the Supreme Court. It wasn’t just a job; it was the peak of years of dedication and hard work.
The confirmation process? It was no walk in the park. But Ruth handled it with the kind of calm, steady determination that had gotten her through so many tough moments before. She spoke honestly about her beliefs, making it clear that fairness and the rule of law were at the heart of everything she did. And you know what? People noticed. Her reputation for integrity and sharp thinking brought her support from all sides.
Once she took her seat on the Supreme Court, things got even more intense. The decisions were bigger, the impact greater, and every word was under the microscope. Ruth quickly made her mark by writing opinions that were thoughtful and clear. But what really set her apart was her courage to speak up—especially when she couldn’t agree with the majority.
Her dissents weren’t just about legal arguments—they carried a powerful sense of right and wrong. Sometimes, Ruth knew the most important thing a judge could do was to stand up and say, “This just isn’t right.”
But Ruth’s influence reached far beyond the courtroom walls. She became a symbol of strength and justice, inspiring people everywhere. Her face popped up on T-shirts and coffee mugs, and her words were shared in speeches and all over social media. She didn’t shy away from being a role model—instead, she used her visibility to encourage others to stand up for what matters.
Despite all the attention, Ruth stayed grounded. She put in long hours, diving deep into every case, reading each brief, and crafting every opinion with care. She also valued her relationships with her colleagues—even those she disagreed with. For Ruth, respect and civility weren’t optional; they were essential, even when opinions clashed.
Ruth’s legacy? It goes way beyond the cases she helped decide. She showed everyone that you could be strong and compassionate at the same time. That you could fight for justice without ever losing sight of what makes us human. Her life proved that persistence, partnership, and sticking to your principles really do matter.
As the world around her kept changing, Ruth stayed steady—a voice for fairness and equality, lighting the way for so many who came after her.

Chapter 6: The Power of Dissent
Imagine being the only person in a room who’s willing to say, “Wait, I see things differently.” That takes a kind of quiet courage, doesn’t it? Ruth Bader Ginsburg knew that feeling well. On the Supreme Court, she often found herself standing alone, especially as the Court’s direction began to shift. And while it might’ve been easier to just go along, Ruth leaned into something she believed deeply—the true power of dissent.
Take this one case, for example. A woman discovered she’d been paid less than her male colleagues for years. But when she finally spoke up, the Court said she’d waited too long to complain. Ruth read that decision and felt a wave of frustration. She understood how discrimination isn’t always obvious—it can hide in everyday moments, and it might take years before someone realizes what’s been happening to them. So, Ruth wrote a dissent that was clear, direct, and full of empathy. She explained, in plain language, how laws should actually help real people—not just work in theory, but in real life.
Now, her words didn’t change the ruling that day. But something fascinating happened: her message reached far beyond the courtroom. People outside the world of law started to notice. Young activists picked up her dissents and saw them as a rallying cry—proof that standing up, even when you’re outnumbered, can make a difference over time. Ruth once said, “Dissent speaks to a future age.” And she meant it. Sometimes, the seeds for real change get planted in those moments of disagreement.
What’s really striking is how Ruth approached dissent. It was never about anger or bitterness. She wrote with respect, always hoping to persuade and to show a better way forward. Over the years, some of her dissents actually inspired new laws and policies. So even when she lost a case, she was still shaping the future—one thoughtful, determined dissent at a time.

Chapter 7: Friendship Across Divides
You know, it’s easy to picture the Supreme Court as a place where conflict never stops—where every conversation is a debate. But Ruth Ginsburg saw things differently. She truly believed in the power of connection, even with people who viewed the world in a totally different way.
One of her closest friendships was with a fellow justice, someone famous for his sharp wit and opinions that often clashed with hers. Sounds unlikely, right? But what made their bond legendary was how they found common ground—like their shared love of opera, laughter, and some pretty spirited debates. Their friendship was this living proof that you can totally disagree, but still care deeply for one another.
Imagine them at the opera, sitting side by side, leaning in close to chat between acts. They might argue fiercely during a session in the courtroom, but then, later on, they’d sit down together for a meal, trading stories and jokes. Ruth really treasured these relationships. She believed that respect and understanding could bridge even the widest divides.
This way of connecting shaped everything she did at the Court. She listened closely to her colleagues, always looking for a bit of common ground. Sometimes, she’d even revise her opinions to address their concerns, hoping to build real consensus. Of course, there were times she stood her ground, but she always did it with civility and grace. Ruth understood that the Court’s authority depended on the public’s trust—and that trust was built on mutual respect among the justices.
For Ruth, these friendships weren’t just about personal warmth. They were part of her bigger vision for a better world. She really wanted people to see that you could disagree—sometimes passionately—without being disagreeable. You could fight for what you believe in, without forgetting the humanity in others.
And in a world where divisions seem to be growing wider every day, Ruth’s example feels more important than ever.

Chapter 8: Facing Loss and Finding Strength
You know, nobody gets through life without facing loss—and Ruth wasn’t any different.
When her beloved partner, Marty, got sick again, it was as if her whole world narrowed down to hospital rooms and those quiet, late-night talks. Marty had always been her anchor—the one who could make her smile, even when things felt impossibly heavy.
His illness really tested her endurance. It was a tough reminder of just how delicate even the closest bonds can be.
Still, Ruth kept moving forward. She’d sit at Marty’s bedside, working late into the night—reading over briefs, writing out court opinions. She found comfort in their routines, and in all the memories they’d made together—those little victories, and the peaceful, everyday moments they’d shared.
When Marty passed away, the grief hit hard. The world felt emptier. The days seemed to stretch on.
But Ruth didn’t pull away. Instead, she chose to honor Marty by pouring herself back into the work they’d both cared so much about. She returned to the Court with her voice as steady as ever. People noticed her resilience—the way she faced each day with quiet grace and determination.
And Ruth didn’t shy away from her pain. She talked about her loss, reminding everyone around her that being vulnerable isn’t a weakness—it’s just part of what it means to be human.
Over the years, Ruth became even more of a symbol. Not just of endurance, but of hope—and of what it really means to keep going when things get tough.
She showed us that real strength isn’t about never falling. It’s about getting up, again and again, no matter how heavy the burden feels.

Chapter 9: Becoming Notorious
It’s funny how life can surprise us, isn’t it? Ruth Bader Ginsburg never set out to become a cultural icon, much less one whose face would show up on T-shirts and murals all across the country. But as the years rolled on, that’s exactly what happened.
Suddenly, young people were wearing her image, artists were painting her into cityscapes, and the name “Notorious RBG” was showing up everywhere online—a clever play on her initials and the famous rapper, Notorious B.I.G. At first, Ruth laughed it off. She saw it as a bit of fun, something lighthearted. But deep down, she understood why it was happening.
There was something about Ruth that made people believe things could get better. She stood as living proof that when you hold onto your convictions and keep pushing forward, one person really can make a difference. And she didn’t shy away from this new spotlight. Instead, she leaned in—meeting with students, giving talks, and urging everyone to use their voices. She talked about why voting matters, why we have to stay informed, and why we should never give up on the promise of equality.
Through it all, Ruth’s humor sparkled. She’d make jokes about her tough workouts, her love for opera, and, of course, her famous collection of lace collars. Yes, she became a pop culture sensation, but she never lost focus on what truly mattered. She used her popularity as a chance to shine a light on issues that deserved attention—to remind people that the fight for justice is ongoing, and every voice counts.
For so many, Ruth became a guiding star—a beacon, really—showing us that change is possible, even when it feels far away. She inspired a whole new generation to believe in the power of law and, even more importantly, to believe in their own ability to shape the world around them.

Chapter 10. The Final Years and Lasting Impact
As Ruth grew older, people couldn’t help but worry about her health. She faced cancer and other illnesses head-on, bringing the same grit and determination she always had in her work. Every time she made her way back to the Supreme Court bench, crowds would cheer—so grateful to see her unwavering commitment in action.
Even in her final years, Ruth never stepped back. She kept writing opinions, mentoring bright young lawyers, and raising her voice for justice and equality. She knew her legacy wasn’t just about court decisions—it lived on in the people she encouraged and in the hope she sparked.
When Ruth passed away, the response was overwhelming. People gathered outside the Supreme Court, leaving flowers, notes, and candles as a tribute. They shared stories—how Ruth inspired them, how her words gave them the courage to stand up and fight for what’s right. Her life became a touchstone, reminding us all of what’s possible when someone refuses to settle for the world as it is, and instead works to make it better.
Ruth’s impact is still felt—in the laws she helped shape, in the doors she opened, and in the example she set. She showed us that justice isn’t just an abstract idea. It’s about daily choices, treating others with dignity, and standing up for what’s right—even when it isn’t easy.

As we wrap up, let’s take a moment to reflect on what Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s story really means for us.
It’s not just a tale about the law, or even about the Supreme Court. It’s about the steady, quiet work of making life a bit fairer—one step at a time.
Her journey shows us that change isn’t usually quick or easy, but it’s always possible. Even when she faced obstacles that might’ve made anyone else give up, she kept moving forward. Why? Because she was guided by a deep sense of justice, and a belief in the power of reason and empathy.
So, here are a few things to take with you:
Real change is built on small, persistent acts of courage and clarity.
Dissent—even when it feels lonely—can plant seeds for progress down the road.
Lasting impact often comes from building respect and friendships across divides.
Strength isn’t about being unbreakable. It’s about finding the courage to keep going, even when you’re vulnerable.
And above all, every voice truly matters in the ongoing journey toward justice and equality.
So, if you ever wonder whether your efforts are making a difference, remember Ruth’s example. She didn’t set out to be a hero—she just did the work in front of her, day after day, with care and conviction.
The world needs people who are willing to listen, to speak up, and to keep trying—even when the odds seem long. Justice isn’t a destination; it’s a journey we all share.
Let Ruth’s story remind you: your actions—no matter how small—can help bend the arc of history toward fairness.
Keep going. The world is waiting.
